feedback.message: Not yet — `@mod` is the remainder that goes with `@divFloor`, and for a positive divisor it is never negative. `@rem` would give −1.

hints: −9 / 4 = −2.25. Truncating goes toward zero; flooring goes down.
`@mod(a, b)` satisfies a = b × @divFloor(a, b) + @mod(a, b).
exercises.solution: It prints `-2 -3 3`. −9 / 4 is −2.25: `@divTrunc` rounds toward zero (−2), `@divFloor` rounds down (−3). `@mod` pairs with floor division: −9 = 4 × (−3) + 3, so it is 3. (`@rem` pairs with truncation and would give −1.)

Not yet — that would be saturating subtraction, `-|`. This is wrapping, `-%`.

hints: `-%=` is wrapping subtraction: the result is taken modulo 2⁸ = 256.
exercises.solution: Wrapping arithmetic on a `u8` works modulo 256, so 10 − 20 = −10 ≡ **246**. With plain `-=` the program would panic with an integer overflow in safe modes; with `-|=` (saturating) it would stop at 0.

exercises.solution: 1, 2 are counted; 3 skipped; 4, 5 counted; 6 skipped; 7, 8 counted; 9 skipped; 10 counted; 11 is not a multiple of 3 and is greater than 10, so the loop breaks. Counted: 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, which is **7**.

The word has 5 letters; `1...4` includes 1 to 4 only, so the `else` prong gives `"long"`. `{}` with no specifier prints a `bool` as `true` or `false`.

exercises.prompt: `a` is a run-time variable of the first type. In which cases does `const b: T = a;` compile **without** a cast? Select all that apply.

options.label: `u8` to `u16`
options.feedback: Yes. Every `u8` value fits in a `u16`.

options.label: `u16` to `u8`
options.feedback: Not yet — 300 is a `u16` that does not fit in a `u8`. You need `@intCast` (checked) or `@truncate`.

options.label: `i8` to `u8`
options.feedback: Not yet — a negative `i8` has no `u8` value. `@intCast` is checked; `@bitCast` reinterprets the bits.

options.label: `u8` to `i16`
options.feedback: Yes. 0 to 255 all fit in a signed 16-bit integer.

options.label: `i32` to `f64`
options.feedback: Yes. A `f64` represents every 32-bit integer exactly, so the coercion is lossless.

options.label: `u64` to `f64`
options.feedback: Not yet — a `f64` has 53 bits of precision, so large `u64` values would be rounded. Use `@floatFromInt` to say you accept that.

hints: Zig coerces only when every value of the source type is exactly representable in the target type.
exercises.solution: (a), (d) and (e) coerce, because every source value is exactly representable in the target type. (b), (c) and (f) can lose information, so Zig makes you write the conversion: `@intCast`, `@truncate`, `@bitCast` or `@floatFromInt`, each of which says something different about what you expect.

exercises.prompt: `x` is a `u32` and `n` is a `u8` read from a file. Why does `x << n` fail to compile, and what is the best fix?

options.label: Shifting a `u32` needs an amount of type `u5` (0 to 31). Check that `n < 32` and convert with `@intCast(n)`, or handle larger values as an error.
options.feedback: Yes. The type rule makes an out-of-range shift impossible to express, so the program must decide what to do with bad input.

options.label: Zig does not allow shifts on run-time values; use multiplication.
options.feedback: Not yet — run-time shifts are fine, as long as the amount has the right type.

options.label: Use `@truncate(n)` to get a `u5`, which always works.
options.feedback: Not yet — it compiles, but a value of 40 would silently become 8. That hides bad input instead of dealing with it.

options.label: Change `x` to a `u8` so the types match.
options.feedback: Not yet — the operands do not need the same type. The amount needs the log₂ type of the value's width.

hints: How many bits does it take to count from 0 to 31?
exercises.solution: The shift amount for a `u32` must be a `u5`, because only 0 to 31 are meaningful. Since `n` comes from a file, it might be larger, so validate it: `if (n >= 32) return error.InvalidShift;` then `x << @intCast(n)`. `@truncate` would compile but quietly turn bad input into a different, wrong shift.
